label: Attempts to Count k-Sets
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 265 to 288, asks a deceptively simple combinatorial question: how many distinct subsets of a planar point set can a line separate off? We frame the chapter as a gap between an upper bound and a lower bound that nobody has yet closed.

label: What Is a k-Set
notes: A k-set is a size-k subset of our points cut off by some open halfplane. We stress that the same k points may be reachable by many lines, but it counts once. The count is over distinct subsets, not over the separating lines themselves.

label: Halving Lines and Edges
notes: When k is half of n, the separated subset and its complement have equal size, giving halving lines. Combinatorially these become halving edges: directed point pairs splitting the rest evenly. Bounding their number is the cleanest model problem of the whole chapter.

label: Duality: k-Levels in Arrangements
notes: Point-line duality turns each point into a line and each k-set boundary into a vertex at level k. The k-level is the polyline of points lying above exactly k of the dual lines, so counting k-sets becomes counting the complexity of one level.

label: The Upper-Bound Problem
notes: We define a_k(n) as the maximum number of k-sets over all n-point configurations. The trivial bound is quadratic; the chapter's challenge is to push the exponent on k well below one, which controls the worst case for halving lines too.

label: Crossing Number Tool
notes: The crossing number inequality says any drawing of a graph with many edges relative to vertices forces a cubic surplus of crossings. We build a graph from k-set edges, bound its crossings geometrically, and invert the inequality to limit edge count.

label: The Lovasz Lemma
notes: Lovasz observed that any fixed line meets the collection of halving edges only a linear number of times. This bounded-crossing property is exactly the geometric input the crossing-number machine needs, and it converts a counting question into an inequality about line stabs.

label: Best Known Upper Bound
notes: Feeding the Lovasz stabbing bound into the crossing-number inequality yields the celebrated planar bound of order n times the cube root of k plus one. This remains, decades later, the best known general upper estimate for the number of k-sets in the plane.

label: The Lower Bound
notes: Constructions show k-sets really can be superlinear. The best lower bound multiplies n by two raised to a slowly growing root-log-k term, proving the truth is not merely linear. The genuine growth rate sits trapped somewhere between this and the cube-root ceiling.

label: Halving Lines Special Case
notes: Setting k to n over two isolates halving lines, the hardest instance. Here the upper bound becomes n to the four-thirds and the lower bound stays mildly superlinear. Closing this single gap would essentially resolve the entire k-set counting problem.

label: Higher Dimensions
notes: In dimension d the same questions return with weaker control. Upper bounds grow with the dimension in the exponent and the gap to known constructions widens sharply. The planar cube-root argument has no clean high-dimensional analogue, leaving the area wide open.

label: Recap and Open Problem
notes: We close by restating the standing gap: cube-root upper bound against root-log lower bound. The exact order of the maximum number of halving lines is one of the most stubborn open problems in combinatorial geometry, and this chapter maps the terrain around it.
